title: A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop
caption: **A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop**: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model's proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model's own report.
alt: Two panels with the same layout and a dashed line separating the proposing tier above from the acting tier below. Panel A, A person closes the loop: a model endpoint labeled answers only sits above the line; a developer labeled carries everything sits below it, sends prompt plus error up to the endpoint and receives a patch, runs commands in a local terminal, and receives the error back. Panel B, A runtime closes the loop: a foundation model labeled holds no authority sits above the line; an agent runtime labeled grants each action sits below it, sends context up and receives a proposal, dispatches to an isolated sandbox along a violet arrow and receives an observation, and the sandbox feeds verifiers labeled tests, linters, whose evidence returns to the runtime.
section: From a Useful Proposal to an Accepted Task {#sec-vol3-intro-existence-moment}
context:
An agentic system comes into existence when software closes this interaction loop. Rather than relying on an engineer to copy prompts and error traces back and forth, the surrounding software feeds the foundation model an objective alongside fresh environmental observations, captures the model's proposed action, dispatches that action, and returns structured execution feedback to guide the next decision.

The surrounding software, the **runtime**\index{Runtime (agent)!definition}, enforces the operational boundary between model reasoning and environment mutation. All execution authority resides with the runtime. Because a model outputs only unstructured text or token streams, generating an operation's name confers no inherent permission to run it. The runtime parses the proposed action, verifies that it complies with current access policies, and dispatches the call through a designated tool. A **tool**\index{Tool!definition} provides a structured interface to an environmental capability, such as reading file contents, editing source code, executing a shell command, or running a test suite. The part of the runtime that drives this loop is often called the agent harness, and @sec-vol3-agent-harness develops it as a component of the runtime rather than a separate system. @Fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control sets the two arrangements side by side. In panel A a developer carries every command and every error by hand; in panel B the runtime dispatches only the actions it grants and routes verifier evidence back to itself rather than trusting the model's account of what happened.

title: The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map
caption: **The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map**: The agent stack structured around traditional computing layers (marked with ≈). The live execution loop (top) executes one task trajectory turn by turn. The across-task loop (bottom) compiles evaluated trajectories into updated model policies and coordinates multi-agent scale. While the architectural analogy provides intuition, the chapters develop each subsystem through its own rigorous systems mechanisms.
alt: Map in two bands. The live loop band, one trajectory turn by turn, holds the model, Part I, approximately a processor; agent memory, Part II, approximately a memory hierarchy; the agent runtime, Part IV, approximately an operating system, spanning the band between them; and tool use, Part III, approximately input and output, connected to a dashed environment box. Every arrow passes through the runtime: proposal and context between model and runtime, stored state and record between memory and runtime, validated call and observation between runtime and tools, and effect and result between tools and environment. Below, an across-tasks band holds learning from trajectories, Part V, approximately recompiling, fed by evaluated trajectories and sending updated weights back to the model along a dashed perimeter arrow, and agents at scale, Part VI, approximately scale-out, drawn as a stack of cards fed by many trajectories at once.
context:
The **stochastic computer**\index{Stochastic computer!definition} names that map (@fig-vol3-stochastic-computer-map).[^fn-stored-program-map] Its upper band is the live execution loop of a single task, and its lower band acts across tasks. In the live band, the foundation model plays the processor; context and external stores play the memory hierarchy, from the active context window to long-term retrieval indices; tools play input and output; and the agent runtime plays the operating system, scheduling model calls, mediating every privileged operation, and enforcing access control. Across tasks, learning from recorded runs plays the role of recompiling a program from measurements of its earlier executions, refining the model's policy without changing the runtime's safety boundaries. Coordinating many agents mirrors scale-out across a network, where agents divide one workload and contend for shared state and resource limits.

[^fn-stored-program-map]: **The Stored-Program Organization**: Von Neumann's 1945 draft report on the EDVAC partitioned a computer into central arithmetic, central control, memory, and input/output organs [@vonneumann1945edvac]. In von Neumann's architecture, central control holds the absolute authority to fetch and execute instructions. In an agentic system, that authority is deliberately inverted: authority resides strictly within the surrounding runtime, while the learned model only proposes actions. Trust is decided outside the processor. \index{Von Neumann architecture!stochastic computer map}

The formal task contract and failure consequences dictate necessary runtime controls. System closure represents the engineering response to these exposures rather than an independent coordinate axis.

context:
[^fn-least-privilege-mediation]: **Least Privilege and Complete Mediation**: Saltzer and Schroeder's foundational protection principles dictate that every program must operate using the smallest set of privileges necessary to complete its task (least privilege), and that every access to every object must be systematically validated (complete mediation) [@saltzer1975]. Validating capability grants on every tool invocation applies both principles to a non-deterministic model whose proposals cannot be inherently trusted. Restricting the task's initial capability grant remains the most dependable technique for minimizing potential damage when runtime verification checks fail to intercept an unsafe request. \index{Least privilege!task grant}

The coordinate space in @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy maps agentic workloads across three operational exposure axes: horizon ($\TurnHorizon$, turns along the horizontal), authority ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$ to $\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$ on the vertical), and carried state ($\StateExposureLevel_0$ to $\StateExposureLevel_3$ on the depth axis). This space functions as an analytical lens rather than a rigid taxonomy: two workloads occupying the exact same cell may still demand different runtime controls if their data sensitivity, tool reliability, or catastrophic failure thresholds diverge. Altering the execution environment can shift a task into a completely different cell even when its foundation model and turn horizon remain identical, as demonstrated in example \ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident}. The four workloads plotted in the space are the book's lighthouse workloads, described in @sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses.

```
title: The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle
caption: **The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle**: Each phase marks a change in which component is responsible, not a mandated scheduler. The runtime assembles context, authorizes requests, records outcomes, and assesses progress; the model only proposes, and only an authorized request reaches a tool. A timed-out tool leaves its outcome unknown, and acceptance requires evidence independent of the model's own report, so exhausted limits end in an unresolved outcome or escalation rather than success.
alt: Six phase boxes arranged in a U, each colored and labeled by the component responsible. Top row, left to right: 1 context assembly, runtime; 2 model invocation, model; 3 validate and authorize, runtime, joined by context and proposal arrows. A bold violet authorized arrow descends from phase 3 to the bottom row, which runs right to left: 4 tool execution, tool; 5 observation and evidence, runtime; 6 assess against contract, runtime, joined by outcome and evidence arrows, with a dotted note under the outcome arrow reading unknown if timed out. A dashed red rejected, no execution arrow runs from phase 3 to phase 5 without touching phase 4. Dashed arrows labeled needs approval from phase 3 and wait from phase 6 lead to a dashed wait box labeled resumes, not an exit. A next-turn arrow returns from phase 6 to phase 1, and phase 6 also leads to a green accept deliverable box, evidence meets contract, and a red stop without acceptance box, unresolved or escalate.
context:
6. **Assess against contract**: The runtime evaluates the updated task state against the acceptance criteria defined in the contract. Depending on the outcome, it can authorize another turn, pause for background jobs, request user clarification, terminate the trajectory as unresolvable, or formally accept the deliverable. This determination rests on verified external evidence and resource constraints rather than model self-reports.

These six phases define boundaries of architectural responsibility rather than a rigid, synchronous scheduler. In production systems, authorized operations may run asynchronously against external services, and model outputs may propose final answers instead of tool calls. While implementations can overlap independent sub-tasks, causality enforces strict ordering constraints: a runtime cannot authorize an action based on observations that arrive after dispatch, nor can it infer the physical outcome of an effect from a proposal alone. @Fig-vol3-ch01-execution-lifecycle draws the phases as a U in which only an authorized request descends from validation to the tool. Its dashed paths carry the exceptions: a policy rejection returns to observation history as error feedback without reaching any tool, approvals and background operations pause the turn, and progress assessment either starts a new turn, accepts the deliverable, or stops without acceptance.

title: The Model Call Surface
caption: **The Model Call Surface**: The request carries messages, tool definitions, and limits into a model with frozen weights, which returns a proposal with a stop reason and usage counts. Every arrow out of the response lands in the agent runtime. The runtime validates and authorizes a tool call before anything runs, returns the result as a new message for the next call, sends a finished answer to verification, and quarantines output cut off at its limit.
alt: Diagram. A request card lists tools and limits above a stack of message slabs labeled system, user, assistant, and tool, the tool slab dashed. An arrow leads to a model box showing tokens y1, y2, y3 drawn one per step with frozen weights, and an arrow leads to a response card with rows for text, tool calls, usage, and a highlighted stop reason row. From the stop reason an arrow drops into an agent runtime region to a route on stop reason box. Its tool call branch goes to validate, authorize, then run in sandbox, and from the sandbox an arrow returns up to the tool slab of the request. Its end of turn branch goes to verify, and its output limit branch goes to a red quarantine box.
context:
Here, `kind` indicates how the runtime parser must interpret the payload. The normalized `status` confirms that the transport and generation protocols completed under the adapter's contract, while `stop_reason` captures the **stop reason**\index{Stop reason!definition} reported by the serving engine. This signal reveals why decoding terminated: whether the model generated a designated tool-call sequence, emitted an end-of-sequence token, or halted because it reached the token ceiling. The `usage` block tallies resource consumption, tracking $\SequenceLength$ input tokens processed and $\OutputLength$ output tokens emitted. Bare $\SequenceLength$ is sequence length throughout this book, here the prompt a call reads; the State levels $\Glyph{S}_0$ to $\Glyph{S}_3$ always carry their subscript. Accurate accounting across invocations prevents context-window overflow and provides the raw telemetry needed to monitor operational costs; when an upstream provider omits token accounting, the runtime must record the usage as missing rather than silently recording zero consumption.

Every path out of the response ends in the runtime, and the stop reason chooses the path (@fig-vol3-model-call-surface). A tool call goes to validation and authorization before anything runs, a finished answer goes to verification, and output cut off at its limit goes to quarantine, where it is kept for diagnosis and never executed (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope states the rule).

title: One Keyword, Two Token Sequences
caption: **One Keyword, Two Token Sequences**: The same Python line, unindented and indented by four spaces, drawn on one character grid, with a compiler lexer's tokens above the characters and a byte-pair tokenizer's tokens below. The lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword and identifier for both lines. The tokenizer absorbs the fourth space into the keyword, so the indented line opens with two tokens that do not appear in the unindented one; only the four tokens after the keyword are shared. Identifiers are from the `cl100k_base` vocabulary.
alt: Two stacked blocks, unindented and indented by four spaces. Each block shows a row of character cells for the line def get_user_id():, with lexer tokens above and byte-pair tokens below, each token spanning the characters it covers. Lexer tokens are def, get_user_id, open parenthesis, close parenthesis, and colon; the indented line adds a dashed indent token over the four spaces. Byte-pair tokens for the unindented line are def 755, space get 636, _user 3398, _id 851, and parentheses colon 4658, labeled 5 tokens. For the indented line they are three spaces 262, space def 711, and the same four tokens, labeled 6 tokens. Tokens 755, 262, and 711 are filled dark; a dashed line marks where the lexer splits the indent from def, which the 711 token straddles. Brackets below mark the two leading tokens, where the fourth space joins the keyword, and the four tokens shared by both lines.
context:
[^fn-bpe-compression-origin]: **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**: The algorithm began as a data-compression scheme that repeatedly replaces the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with an unused symbol [@gage1994bpe]; @sennrich2016subword repurposed the same merge rule to build open vocabularies for neural translation. Because the merges are learned from the training corpus's frequencies, the token cost of a string reflects how common it was in that corpus, so an unusual identifier or path can split into more tokens than a common word of the same length, and the runtime must count rather than estimate. \index{Byte-pair encoding!compression origin}

Indentation alone alters the resulting sequence. Under one widely used byte-pair vocabulary, `cl100k_base`, for example, the unindented line `def get_user_id():` encodes as five tokens beginning with `def` (identifier 755). Indenting that exact line by four spaces yields six tokens: three leading spaces (262), followed by ` def` with the fourth space fused to the keyword (711), and finally the remaining four tokens. A compiler lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword token at both levels; the model instead receives a different opening sequence of integer identifiers, with only the four tokens after the keyword shared (@fig-vol3-token-ast-mismatch).
```

title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
caption: **Grammar-Constrained Decoding**: A tool schema compiles once into an automaton whose states each carry a token mask. At every step the mask sets illegal tokens to $-\infty$ before normalization, so only a legal continuation can be drawn, and the drawn token advances the automaton. The logit values are illustrative: a fluent but illegal continuation can outscore the legal one and still receive zero probability. A precomputed per-state mask suits a finite-state constraint; nested structures need additional parser state. The strip along the bottom lists what the mask leaves unchecked.
alt: Diagram. Top: a tool schema with query and limit fields compiles into an automaton with states q0, q1, q2, and final state qF, joined by edges labeled opening brace and query. Above each state sits a strip of mask bits; the strips for q0 and q1 show a few legal bits filled, and q0 is highlighted as the current state. A lookup arrow runs from q0 to an operator plus M of q0 between two bar charts. The left chart, logits z_t, shows illustrative scores SELECT +14.2, I think +18.5, opening brace +8.1, and Sure +12.0. The right chart, masked z prime t, shows SELECT, I think, and Sure as dashed outlines marked minus infinity and only the opening brace bar solid at +8.1. The sampled token y_t, an opening brace, feeds an arrow back up to state q1, labeled advance to q1. A dashed strip at the bottom reads not checked by the mask: table exists, values right, call authorized.
context:
Setting the logits of invalid tokens to $-\infty$ forces their sampling probabilities to zero, renormalizing the distribution entirely across viable continuations. Once the sampler draws a token from this restricted set, the engine consumes that token's characters and advances the parser to state $\DecodingConstraintState_{t+1}$. This formulation assumes that $\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$ remains nonempty and that the sampling configuration respects the mask. The engine applies the mask before top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$ or nucleus truncation so that these filters select among legal continuations. If an implementation instead truncates first and no retained token belongs to $\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$, the serving runtime must raise an explicit constraint-satisfaction error rather than silently disabling the mask. Positive finite temperature rescales the remaining probabilities without removing their support.

Recomputing $\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$ from scratch at every step would cost a scan of the whole vocabulary per token. Engines therefore compile the tool schema once into an automaton whose states each carry a precomputed mask $\LogitMask(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$, so that each step is a lookup followed by a state transition [@willard2023outlines]. Incremental parsing of this kind yields syntactically valid output even for a language as structured as SQL [@scholak2021picard]. The automaton in @fig-vol3-grammar-constrained-fsm is compiled for a query tool with two fields, `query` and `limit`, rather than for `read_file`; the mechanism is identical.

title: Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It
caption: **Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It**: Both paths start from the same connection-pool failure. On the left, generation builds on the timeout explanation without any observation that separates it from a missed notification, so the patch can hide the symptom while the defect remains. On the right, a targeted test orders a waiting worker and a returning connection, and its observation contradicts the timeout explanation before any edit. The revised candidate passes the reproducer, which still falls short of task acceptance.
alt: Two lanes below a box reading observed failure, request waits after a connection frees. The left lane, labeled commit first, holds H1 timeout too short with H2 missed notification drawn faded and dashed, then generate on H1 with no new evidence, then a timeout patch applied unchecked, ending in a red box reading symptom masked, notification defect remains. The right lane, labeled check first, holds both H1 and H2, then an amber targeted test observing the waiter still blocked after return, then the hypotheses again with H1 struck through and marked contradicted, then a notify on return patch, the revised candidate from H2, ending in a green box reading reproducer passes, acceptance still pending. A dashed horizontal line labeled first edit crosses both lanes: the left lane reaches it with no check, the right lane only after the test.
context:
This division marks the operational boundary between internal computation and empirical observation. Additional model computation re-evaluates information already present in the prompt context. Within a single generation, a model can backtrack and revise an earlier analytical misstep even as the previous tokens remain frozen in its context prefix. However, pure computation cannot generate new empirical facts. Only an executed test reports how the running process behaves, and its conclusions remain strictly bounded by the specific conditions and interleavings that the test harness exercised.

Suppose the targeted test forces an interleaving where a worker thread waits while another returns a connection. The execution trace reveals that the connection successfully enters the pool, yet the waiting worker remains blocked past the notification point. This empirical finding rules out the timeout hypothesis immediately and directs the agent toward the synchronization path. The agent can then synthesize a patch that repairs the signaling logic and verify it against the failing reproducer. Passing a targeted reproducer, however, does not constitute full task acceptance; narrow tests can overlook edge cases, and neither an unverified hypothesis nor an isolated micro-test provides sufficient confidence to ship code to production. The two paths part ways before any file changes (@fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree). Acting on the first guess hides the symptom and keeps the defect, whereas checking first spends one short test to learn which hypothesis survives.

```
title: Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection
caption: **Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection**: A qualitative sketch of the measured best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ pattern. The proxy score of the selected candidate keeps rising as $\CandidatePoolSize$ grows, while a held-out reference score rises and then declines. The widening gap illustrates proxy optimism under selection; the declining reference score is an empirical pattern, not a necessary consequence of growing scoring error. The axes carry no values, and the point where the reference score turns down depends on the task.
alt: Line sketch with candidates selected from, N, on a log-scale horizontal axis and score of the selected candidate on the vertical axis, without tick values. A dashed blue curve labeled proxy score rises and flattens. A solid green curve labeled held-out reference follows it at first, peaks near the middle at a marked dot, and then declines. The region between the curves is shaded, a red double-headed arrow at the right labels the gap scoring error of the winner, and a dashed line below the green peak notes that where the decline begins depends on the task.
context:
[^fn-gumbel-tail-growth]: **Extreme-Value Asymptotics**: The form $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$ is only the leading term of the Gaussian maximum, and convergence is slow, which is why the chapter computes the exact expectation beside it. The Gaussian is also a favorable case. Scoring errors with heavier tails, such as a learned judge that occasionally misjudges badly, push the selected error up faster than $\sqrt{\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$, so the drift in a real pool can exceed this estimate. \index{Extreme value!argmax selection}

Rising selected scoring error does not by itself imply declining true utility. In Exercise 8(b), independent Gaussian utility and noise make both the winner's expected utility and its scoring error increase with pool size. Empirical evaluations of best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling against learned reward models show a different pattern. The optimized proxy score keeps increasing while an independent reference score initially improves, plateaus, and eventually degrades [@gao2023scaling]. That downturn depends on the joint distribution of utility and measurement error, or on checks that search can exploit; @eq-vol3-argmax-noise alone does not predict it. @Fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence sketches the empirical pattern, with a rising proxy score (dashed blue curve) and a held-out reference score (solid green curve) that peaks before declining.

title: Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration
caption: **Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration**: In (A), the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis. Following the recorded dependency edges marks the patch and check selection for review, while the recorded inputs and the separately derived API notes keep their support. In (B), a new request supplies that supported frontier and regenerates only the diagnosis, patch, and check selection. The graph records candidate artifacts, not executed operations, and each replacement must still pass its own checks. The test inventory that also feeds check selection is omitted.
alt: Two stacked panels with the same dependency graph. Inputs on the left are source excerpt, failure observation, waiter-return test, and API declaration. In panel A, source excerpt and failure observation feed a red diagnosis marked timeout too short, which feeds a patch candidate and then a check selection; source excerpt also feeds the patch candidate. The patch candidate and check selection are drawn with dashed red borders, labeled needs review, inside a dashed region labeled Desc of diagnosis. The waiter-return test points to the diagnosis with a dashed red arrow labeled contradicts. The API declaration feeds API notes labeled support kept. In panel B, a dashed blue region labeled regenerated contains diagnosis prime labeled missed notification, patch candidate prime labeled notify on return, and check selection prime labeled ordering test; the same inputs, now including the waiter-return test, feed diagnosis prime, and API notes are labeled retained.
context:
When an input artifact changes or an assumption fails, the runtime marks that node as unsupported and traverses the dependency edges to identify all downstream artifacts requiring re-evaluation. If an artifact node $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ loses its supporting evidence, the set of invalidated artifacts is precisely its reachable descendants in the graph: $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode) = \{\ReachableArtifactNode \mid \InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode\}$, where $\InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode$ indicates that a directed path leads from $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ to $\ReachableArtifactNode$. A breadth-first search computes $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ in time linear in the number of vertices and edges.[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies] All nodes outside $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ retain their validity, preserving independent subgraphs such as the API compatibility analysis. A candidate graph of dozens or hundreds of nodes, like the schema in @tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies, is traversed in a tiny fraction of the illustrative `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` it takes to generate a single token. The engineering burden therefore lies not in graph search but in capturing dependency edges accurately. The numerator is a gain in the estimated probability of an acceptable result, not a count of new candidates or a rise in scorer output, and the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) is the reason. Producing another candidate and establishing that some candidate is valid are different events, so progress has to be measured by the second. A search that keeps generating while its calibrated acceptance estimate stays flat is spending without progress, however much output it produces. The threshold is an economic choice rather than a property of the search algorithm. The value of an additional acceptable result relative to escalation, including residual checker error and delay, sets the threshold. Severe failure costs do not by themselves justify more search against an unreliable check.

For satisficing policies, runtimes must enforce these stopping rules according to a strict three-tier precedence (@fig-vol3-stopping-boundaries). Hard resource limits on tokens, API requests, search depth, and wall-clock deadlines take absolute precedence and stop new admissions unconditionally. The runtime preserves any candidate that already meets the acceptance criteria for the acceptance decision; without one, it reports an unresolved outcome or escalates. Satisficing rules evaluate second. Any candidate satisfying full acceptance criteria terminates search within the available resource envelope. The marginal stopping rule of @eq-vol3-marginal-stopping applies last, governing continuation only when hard limits remain unreached and no candidate has yet met acceptance criteria. Inverting this hierarchy would permit speculative value estimates to breach hard resource quotas, or allow diminishing marginal returns to abandon an already successful candidate.
```

caption: **Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token**: Three consecutive requests follow the root, trunk, and leaf order of @tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ beyond the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$. A new observation changes only the leaf, so the root and trunk remain a reusable prefix. context:
Request organization directly governs inference performance and cost. Serving engines equipped with prefix caching[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse] skip redundant prefill computation by reusing the key-value (KV) attention state of an identical leading token sequence. Because causal self-attention computes each token's keys and values from all preceding tokens, a single changed token near the beginning invalidates the cached state for every later position, even when thousands of trailing tokens are identical. Attention state is derived from the token prefix (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). Ordering the zones by change rate is what turns this rule into savings. A call that changes only the leaf reuses the root and trunk, whereas a compaction that rewrites the trunk ends reuse at the root boundary and forces recomputation of every later token (@fig-vol3-context-zones).

[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse]: **Automatic Prefix Reuse**: Serving systems such as SGLang index cached attention state by token prefix within a radix tree, allowing an incoming request that shares an existing token prefix to reuse cached KV blocks transparently [@zheng2024sglang]. Because radix tree lookups evaluate exact token equality rather than semantic equivalence, two requests that diverge on an early timestamp share zero cache entries past that offset. Layout discipline directly determines cache hit rates. \index{Prefix cache!radix tree}

title: Block Table Indirection and Tail Copy-on-Write
caption: **Block Table Indirection and Tail Copy-on-Write**: Panel (a) follows each logical block through its table entry to a physical block scattered among other requests' blocks; position 9 resolves to logical block 2, then to physical block 9, slot 1. Panel (b) shows two candidates that share the full blocks 3 and 7, while candidate B's private append first copies the two initialized entries of the shared tail into block 14.

The path for position 9 is drawn in dark ink and annotated with the floor of 9 over 4 equals 2, table entry 2 equals 9, and slot 9 mod 4 equals 1. Panel b places candidate A's block table 3, 7, 9 above and candidate B's table 3, 7, 14 below; both tables point to the shared blocks 3 and 7, A points to block 9, and an arrow copies slots 0 and 1 from block 9 into block 14, where B writes position 10.
context:
Consider an illustrative block size of four tokens, chosen to make the mapping concrete rather than to recommend a production configuration. A ten-token prefix occupies logical blocks 0, 1, and 2. Its block table contains `[3, 7, 9]`: token positions 0–3 reside in physical block 3, positions 4–7 in block 7, and positions 8–9 in the first two slots of block 9. Physical block IDs are pool indices managed by the allocator, not raw memory addresses or token sequence numbers.

For any token position, the attention kernel determines its logical block index via integer division by the block size, consults the block table to locate the physical block, and calculates the token's offset within that block using the modulo remainder. For token position 9 with a four-token block size, the kernel calculates logical block $\lfloor 9 / 4 \rfloor = 2$, looks up physical block 9, and determines offset $9 \bmod 4 = 1$ (the second slot). Computing the final byte offset in device memory incorporates the model layer, KV head index, and tensor stride conventions. This software lookup preserves logical sequence ordering even when physical blocks are scattered across high-bandwidth memory among other requests' blocks, as panel (a) of @fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping traces for position 9.

title: Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache
caption: **Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache**: Each node stands for a run of tokens and the KV blocks that hold them, so a request's cached state is the path from the root to its node. Nodes on a running request's path stay active. Only dormant leaves are eligible, which is why the dormant Other-task node in panel (a) survives until its Final-turn child is evicted in panel (b). A least-recently-used policy would choose among the eligible leaves; it never removes an ancestor before its retained descendants.
alt: Two stacked copies of a three-level tree, panel a above panel b, whose nodes each carry a small row of KV block squares. Panel a has an active shared-prefix root, an active repair-history node with an active test-log-turn leaf and a dormant rejected-branch leaf, and a dormant other-task node with a dormant final-turn leaf; thicker green edges trace the running request's path, and the two dormant leaves are shaded gray with dark dashed borders as eligible for eviction. Panel b shows the final-turn leaf faded with dotted borders as evicted and the other-task node now shaded as an eligible dormant leaf. A legend defines active, dormant, eligible, and evicted.
context:
Reusing and reclaiming memory blocks requires strict ownership tracking across concurrent threads and hardware streams. When a request matches a cached prefix, the memory manager increments reference counts on the corresponding blocks before dispatching execution kernels. Conversely, before reclaiming a physical block under memory pressure, the allocator must sever the cache's indexing reference, confirm that active execution references have dropped to zero, and synchronize with outstanding device streams that might still be reading or writing those memory addresses. The allocator must also synchronize index modifications and reference changes so that a concurrent lookup cannot bind to a block while background eviction is tearing it down.

In tree-structured prefix caches, **leaf-first eviction**\index{Leaf-first eviction!definition} maintains structural consistency by preserving contiguous paths from the root and evicting unused leaf nodes first. Because internal nodes store common prefix state shared across multiple conversation branches, evicting an ancestor would invalidate all of its downstream descendants. An internal node becomes eligible for reclamation only after all of its descendant children have been evicted. Within the set of eligible leaves, systems frequently adopt a least-recently-used (LRU) policy [@zheng2024sglang], operating on the premise that recent access predicts near-term reuse [@belady1966study].[^fn-lru-belady-optimal] Reclamation therefore cascades upward. An inactive parent cannot be reclaimed while its child remains cached, but once the child leaf is evicted, the parent itself becomes an eligible leaf and can be freed if memory pressure persists (@fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache).

context:
If the engine can predict the tool completion timestamp accurately, typically from a hint the agent runtime supplies, asynchronous prefetching can schedule the inward transfer to complete precisely as the test finishes. Reserving the destination device blocks at the start of that inbound copy yields an accelerator release window of `{python} PausedStateChoice.wait_str` $-$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.out_str` $-$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.in_str` $=$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.prefetch_free_str`. Prefetching hides restoration latency completely while maintaining both transfer stages, though it requires reliable advance knowledge of return times.

The same reasoning extends to every context length and wait. The round-trip transfer time, which scales linearly with context length and equals `{python} PausedStateChoice.transfer_str` in this configuration, sets a necessary condition. A pause shorter than the round trip ends before offloading can move the state out and back without delaying resumption. Keeping it avoids restoration work when memory permits; under pressure, moving or dropping it may still be necessary. Above the round trip, offloading becomes possible, and whether it pays depends on whether other requests are queued for the freed memory and how much reload delay the resuming turn tolerates. For long pauses under memory pressure, offloading reclaims device memory for almost the entire wait at the cost of a sub-second reload. The worked `{python} PausedStateChoice.context_str`-token, `{python} PausedStateChoice.wait_str` test sits far beyond that round trip. It also sits short of the much longer waits at which parked state accumulates enough to fill host memory, a boundary set by host capacity and by how fast paused trajectories arrive rather than by a fixed duration. The example therefore falls squarely in the offload regime (@fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff). When pauses stretch into minutes or hours, as for operations awaiting human review, parked state accumulates in host memory, and the decision turns on host capacity, secondary storage bandwidth, or eventual recomputation.

A structural index (B) records parsed containment and resolved calls, here from the waiter test to the pool's return method and on to its notification call. Its coverage is declared rather than complete, because a dynamic call can leave a target unresolved.

Panel A, lexical index, shows three quoted terms, notify, waiter, and return, each with an arrow to two postings naming a file and a term frequency; the notify row and its postings src/pool.py 2 and r17.log 1 are highlighted and labeled source and failure log alike, with a note that a match is an occurrence, not a relationship. Lexical matches identify raw text occurrences. **Structural retrieval**\index{Structural retrieval!definition} distinguishes program organization: the enclosing function, type declarations, lexical scopes, and identifiers in call expressions. A parser translates source text into abstract syntax trees with explicit spans, while symbol resolution and semantic analysis establish directed relationships between definitions and call sites. While parsing a call expression identifies the call site syntactically, resolving which concrete implementation executes at runtime requires interprocedural analysis.

During the connection-pool repair, a structural query can return the entire function containing a notification call in `src/pool.py` rather than an arbitrary fragment, and a reference query can subsequently identify its callers across the codebase. Static coverage depends on language semantics, dependencies, and build configuration; dynamic dispatch, reflection, generated code, and cross-process calls frequently escape static resolution. In a structural index, a missing edge indicates a gap in static coverage rather than an unreachable path, while a static call edge records a potential invocation rather than an executed one. The two representations see the pool's sources differently (@fig-vol3-lexical-vs-ast). A lexical index finds the term `notify` in the pool source and the r17 failure log alike, whereas a structural index records that the waiter test calls the pool's return method, which in turn calls the notification, a caller-callee chain that string matching cannot recover.

title: Searching an HNSW Graph
caption: **Searching an HNSW Graph**: Each upper layer holds a geometrically smaller subset of the vectors. The query enters at the top, hops greedily toward $\SearchQueryEmbedding$ until no neighbor is closer, and drops a layer from that node. In layer 0 the walk widens into a beam of width $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ that visits more nodes than it returns and yields the best $\RetrievalCutoffCount$. A vector the beam never visits cannot be returned, which is where approximate search misses come from.
alt: Three stacked tilted planes labeled layer 2 (few vectors), layer 1 (more vectors), and layer 0 (every vector, up to M links each), drawn over one shared point layout so each upper layer shows a subset of the same vectors, with a dashed query marker q at the same position in every plane. In layer 2 a blue arrow hops from the entry point to a node nearer q, and a dashed arrow labeled no closer neighbor: drop falls straight down to the same node in layer 1; after a second hop, another dashed arrow labeled drop: beam starts here falls to layer 0. In layer 0 green links and outlined nodes mark the nodes the beam visited around q and three filled green nodes mark the returned nodes; the remaining gray nodes were never visited. A key identifies greedy hop, visited by beam with width ef search, returned best k, and never visited.
context:
\HnswLevelDraw \cdot \HnswLevelNormalization \rfloor$, where $\HnswLevelDraw$ is drawn uniformly from $(0, 1]$ and $\HnswLevelNormalization = 1 / \ln \HnswMaximumConnectionCount$, with $\HnswMaximumConnectionCount$ defining the maximum number of bidirectional connections per node per layer. The assignment gives each vector probability $\HnswMaximumConnectionCount^{-\HnswLayerIndex}$ of reaching layer $\HnswLayerIndex$ or above, so each layer holds roughly $1/\HnswMaximumConnectionCount$ as many nodes as the one beneath it, an exponentially thinning hierarchy that mirrors the express transit lanes of a skip list [@pugh1990skip]. Traversal begins at an entry point in the sparsest top layer, greedily hopping to whichever neighbor minimizes distance to the query vector $\SearchQueryEmbedding$. When no neighbor yields further progress, the search drops down to that node's counterpart in the next layer and resumes the greedy walk. Upon reaching layer 0, the traversal switches from greedy routing to a beam search that maintains a priority queue of the $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ closest candidates discovered so far. The search terminates when the closest unexplored neighbor cannot improve the current candidate set, returning the top $\RetrievalCutoffCount$ vectors. The beam width $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ is the primary query-time recall knob. A vector the beam never visits cannot be returned (@fig-vol3-hnsw-routing), so widening the beam evaluates more distances and recovers more true neighbors at the cost of higher query latency.

Constructing an HNSW graph requires executing this layered search for every incoming vector and establishing bidirectional links to its nearest neighbors in each layer. This graph topology incurs substantial memory overhead beyond the raw vectors. Deletions are harder still, because severing a node without reconstructing edge paths among its neighbors risks partitioning the graph and stranding downstream vectors. Production systems therefore mark a deleted node with a tombstone, an exclusion marker that hides it from results while its links stay in place, and @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation examines how the cost of that compromise compounds.

At query time the full-precision query selects the $\ProbedCellCount$ nearest cells, fills a table of distances to every subspace centroid, and scores each stored code with $\PqSubvectorCount$ table lookups. Sizes follow the exact-scan notebook's corpus.

$$ {#eq-vol3-pq-adc}

@Eq-vol3-pq-adc transforms a bandwidth-bound $\EmbeddingDimension$-component dot product into $\PqSubvectorCount$ single-byte reads and table lookups. Because the lookup table is small enough to stay in processor cache, each scored vector costs $\PqSubvectorCount$ bytes of memory traffic instead of $\EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize$, a reduction by the factor $\EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize/\PqSubvectorCount$ in exactly the term that bounded the exact scan. The parameter $\ProbedCellCount$ balances recall against the number of cells scanned, while the subvector count $\PqSubvectorCount$ trades distance fidelity against bytes per code. Systems commonly recover distance accuracy by re-scoring a short candidate list against full-precision vectors stored on secondary media or remote memory. The same design scales to billions of vectors on accelerators [@johnson2019billion]. The quantization codebooks and coarse centroids, however, are calibrated on the vector distribution present during index construction; as the corpus drifts or the embedding model changes, quantization error grows until the index is retrained.

title: Filtering Inside a Graph Walk
caption: **Filtering Inside a Graph Walk**: A scope mask applied during traversal (A) removes the only links between the entry region and the eligible vectors nearest $\SearchQueryEmbedding$, so the greedy walk stops at a local minimum and returns too few results even though eligible neighbors exist. The three responses (B) partition the index along scope boundaries, restart the walk from an entry point inside the eligible region, or, when the filter is selective, score every eligible vector exactly.
alt: Two panels. Panel A, mask applied during the walk, shows a graph split by a shaded vertical band labeled scope mask that contains dashed gray masked nodes. A blue arrow from an entry node reaches a green node circled in red and labeled stalls here; every link from the left eligible nodes to the right side passes through masked nodes, and the green nodes near a dashed query marker q on the right are labeled eligible near q, unreachable. Panel B, three responses, shows three rows: partition by scope, with separate graphs for scope X (green) and scope Y (gray dashed); extra entry point, where a blue entry node labeled extra entry starts the walk among green nodes near q; and exact scan when selective, with q and an arrow labeled score all pointing to a box of five green nodes.
context:
Selecting among these index structures requires evaluating them against the specific record volumes, query distributions, and latency budgets the agent encounters. Systems engineers must also distinguish two evaluation metrics. Recall against an exact scan measures algorithmic fidelity to the mathematical distance metric, whereas end-to-end task success measures whether the retrieved records contain the requisite causal evidence to resolve the agent's objective.

The filtering hazard from lexical search (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-search-scope) returns here in sharper form, because scope filters present greater friction on a graph index than on inverted postings lists. In lexical retrieval, intersecting a postings list with an eligibility bitset prunes unauthorized documents without altering how the remaining documents are traversed. In an HNSW graph, restricting search during traversal (pre-filtering) forces the beam to step exclusively onto eligible nodes. If a tenant boundary or file path mask isolates regions of the graph, the greedy walk stalls at a local minimum when all outgoing links lead to masked nodes. The search terminates prematurely and returns incomplete results, even when highly relevant eligible nodes exist just beyond the masked barrier. Conversely, filtering after an unconstrained search (post-filtering) risks returning an empty set whenever the top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ candidates fall outside the authorized scope. Systems escape the dilemma in one of three ways (@fig-vol3-access-prefilter). They partition the index into scope-isolated subgraphs, seed extra entry points inside the authorized region, or fall back to an exact scan when the filter is selective enough that the measured full request meets the budget, using the floor in notebook \ref{nbk-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor} as an initial feasibility screen.

A cross-encoder reorders only a short pool, because its work grows with both pool size and pair length, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget.

```

The substantial computational demand of this joint pass is why rerankers operate exclusively on short candidate pools. In a bi-encoder design, candidate vectors are computed offline, reducing query-time evaluation to a lightweight vector dot product. In a cross-encoder, query and candidate tokens must be processed jointly through the transformer layers, preventing offline precomputation. Computational cost scales with both candidate pool depth and token sequence length. For example, reranking a pool of `{python} RerankPool.pool_str` candidates of `{python} RerankPool.passage_str` tokens each against a `{python} RerankPool.query_str`-token query requires processing `{python} RerankPool.total_str` tokens, a prefill load comparable to a substantial model call, spent entirely on ordering. Systems manage this latency budget by constraining candidate pool sizes, invoking rerankers conditionally based on query ambiguity, or executing reranking asynchronously off the interactive path. The complete hybrid pipeline therefore narrows as it proceeds (@fig-vol3-hnsw-rrf). Two candidate generators feed a fusion step that needs only ranks, the costly reranker sees only the short fused pool, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget.

title: The tool-call loop
caption: **The tool-call loop**: Validation and authorization can reject a proposed call before dispatch. For a dispatched call, the runtime tracks the available outcome and shapes the return into a bounded observation matched to its call identifier. An unknown effect remains unknown in that observation.
alt: Loop diagram. A model box for turn t holds call_1, call_2, and call_3 and sends calls into a runtime container, which sits between the model and a tool or environment box where the effect lands. Inside the runtime, validate, authorize, and dispatch run left to right; dispatch reaches the tool, and the raw return comes back into a shape stage. Dashed red arrows from validate, labeled invalid, and from authorize, labeled not granted, go straight down into the context for turn t+1, which holds one slot per call ID: an error for call_3 from validate, an error for call_2 from authorize, and a result for call_1 from the shape stage. An arrow labeled next turn returns from the context to the model.
context:
Following authorization, dispatch submits the permitted operation to the underlying execution provider while outcome tracking maintains execution identity and status. This tracking distinguishes among pre-dispatch rejections, active background tasks, successfully reported results, and unconfirmed execution states. A transport timeout indicates only that the runtime exceeded its waiting deadline, leaving the remote execution state unconfirmed. Finally, observation shaping maps the raw return value back to the originating call identifier, truncating payloads to fit context budgets, sanitizing terminal escape sequences, and tagging the output with accurate status metadata. If log output must be truncated, the payload explicitly discloses the omission; if a system returns an asynchronous job ticket, observation shaping reports it as an acknowledgment rather than a completed effect.

Certain validation checks must execute at the remote endpoint because safety requires atomicity with the state change itself; for example, an edit conditioned on a source version requires the version check to occur in lockstep with the update. Consequently, the host runtime and the remote endpoint each enforce their respective boundaries. The endpoint checks access independently, even for requests that the host runtime already cleared. This division is the end-to-end argument applied to system protection. An authorization check that depends on private endpoint state can be finalized only at that endpoint, which makes preliminary host-level checks useful optimizations rather than authoritative substitutes [@saltzer1984endtoend].

title: One operation, many attempts
caption: **One operation, many attempts**: The runtime creates the operation ID once and gives each attempt a fresh attempt ID, so a timeout leads either to another attempt of the same intent or, once attempts run out, to an unresolved outcome. The endpoint's lookup, scoped to caller and resource within its retention window, decides whether a request returns a retained result, a pending status, or an ID conflict, or executes. Only the last branch applies the effect. Recording the result inside the same transaction boundary, where the effect permits one, keeps a crash from leaving an applied effect without the record that deduplicates its retries.
alt: Two-part flow diagram. On the left, a runtime column: admit intent creates the op ID once; attempt k, drawn as a stack of cards, keeps the same op ID with a new attempt ID; a red timeout box with effect unknown loops back to the attempt and leads, dashed, to an unresolved box once attempts are exhausted. A request arrow goes to an endpoint lookup of the op ID scoped to caller, resource, and retention window, and a dashed reply returns. The lookup fans out to four outcomes: completed returns the retained result, still running returns a pending status, payload differs is an ID conflict, and not found executes. A bracket marks the first three as no new effect; only not found continues into a dashed box labeled one transaction, which holds apply effect followed by record result.
context:
An operation identifier provides safety only when governed by an explicit endpoint contract. This contract binds the operation ID to the caller's identity, the target resource scope, and the serialized payload. If a client reuses an active operation ID with mismatched arguments, the endpoint must reject the request with a client error (such as an HTTP 409 Conflict) rather than silently dispatching a mutated operation. Furthermore, the endpoint must enforce access control independently on each attempt, because possessing a valid operation token does not substitute for authorized credentials when dispatching actions or retrieving retained execution results.

The contract must also govern concurrent and interleaved requests. If a duplicate request arrives while the original attempt is actively executing, the endpoint should return an in-progress or pending status instead of spawning a parallel worker. If a duplicate arrives after execution finishes, the endpoint returns the previously computed and retained result. To uphold this guarantee under crash failures, the endpoint's persistence mechanism must atomically link the side effect with its stored completion record. If a worker applies the mutation and crashes before persisting the result, a simple log of request receipt cannot prove that re-execution is safe. Where the underlying resource supports it, enclosing both the mutation and the result record within a single database transaction guarantees atomic state transitions. When acting against external services lacking transactional boundaries, the endpoint must coordinate with the downstream system's native deduplication mechanisms. Every request therefore ends in one of four outcomes of the endpoint's lookup, and only an unseen operation ID executes (@fig-vol3-idempotency-flow).

title: Bounded capture before staging
caption: **Bounded capture before staging**: The adapter drains each bounded pipe from one readiness loop, so neither channel stalls the child, and enforces a byte limit and a deadline on capture. The head fills once, the tail ring overwrites its oldest bytes, and the middle is counted but not kept, so capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes. The staged observation carries status, head, a notice of the measured omission, and tail within the byte budget $\ObservationByteBudget$; a retained record, when authorized, lets later calls read omitted ranges by handle.
alt: Datapath diagram. A child process writes stdout and stderr into an adapter, where both bounded pipes feed one readiness loop labeled byte limit and deadline. The loop emits an output stream of any length, drawn as a bar along a time axis: a head segment, a long hatched middle that is counted but not kept, and a tail segment. Below it, a fixed-size capture memory holds a full linear head buffer, an omission count that keeps no bytes, and a tail ring buffer that overwrites its oldest slots. The buffers feed a staged observation stacked as status, head, a dashed notice of bytes omitted, tail, and handle; below the stack, the equation M obs,max equals M head plus M notice plus M tail, and an arrow leads to the next model call, measured in tokens. A dashed retained record, if authorized, serves range reads to the handle.
context:
$$\ObservationByteBudget = \HeadByteAllocation + \NoticeByteAllocation + \TailByteAllocation$$ {#eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget}

In @eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget, $\HeadByteAllocation$ reserves space for the initial execution prefix, $\NoticeByteAllocation$ allocates bytes for an explicit truncation disclaimer, and $\TailByteAllocation$ preserves the most recent output suffix. The adapter implements this with fixed memory overhead: $\HeadByteAllocation$ bytes are captured into a linear buffer until full, after which incoming bytes feed a ring buffer of size $\TailByteAllocation$. The omission counter increases only when a byte is evicted from that ring, so bytes still retained in the tail are not counted as dropped. When the child process exits, the adapter serializes the head buffer, an omission notice detailing the exact count of dropped bytes, and the ring buffer in chronological order, so capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes (@fig-vol3-stream-ingestion).

title: Shallow and deep interfaces for one edit
caption: **Shallow and deep interfaces for one edit**: The low-level composition (a) spends four model calls and places a handle, a cursor, and cleanup in the trajectory between them. The task-level operation (b) spends one call and moves the version check and the change behind the interface, returning either a diff with its new version or a version conflict. The deeper interface is all-or-nothing only if its implementation provides that property; either way, the obligations move rather than disappear.
alt: Two stacked panels, each with a trajectory row above a dashed interface line and a tool row below it. Panel a, low-level composition, labeled 4 model calls: four call boxes along the trajectory, each with a round trip down to one tool operation, open_file, seek_cursor, write_bytes, and close_file; small chips between the calls carry a handle, a cursor, and cleanup along the trajectory. Panel b, task-level operation, labeled 1 model call: one call box goes down to a single apply_patch operation that contains check version followed by apply change; check version returns a version conflict and apply change returns a diff and new version, both back above the interface line.
context:
that effective module boundaries hide design decisions that are subject to change [@parnas1972criteria], and Ousterhout formalized this criterion through deep vs. shallow interfaces, measuring how much implementation complexity an abstraction hides relative to the surface area it exposes [@ousterhout2018philosophy]. The same principles hold in agent systems, where tool interfaces designed around an agent's editing, navigation, and testing patterns raised task success rates on software engineering benchmarks [@yang2024sweagent]. A **deep interface**\index{Deep interface!definition} encapsulates substantial functionality behind a concise contract, whereas a shallow interface exposes almost as much complexity as it implements. For example, a file-editing interface built from discrete `open_file`, `seek_cursor`, `write_bytes`, and `close_file` operations forces the model to manage low-level file descriptors, cursor offsets, and resource cleanup across the trajectory. Such fine-grained decomposition is warranted only when intermediate inspection is an explicit requirement; when the agent merely intends to apply a bounded patch, this overhead invites state corruption and premature failure.

A task-level patch operation moves mechanical file manipulation behind the tool implementation, returning a unified diff, a resulting version hash, or an explicit conflict. The conditional-edit contract in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas illustrates this boundary. However, interface naming alone does not guarantee transactional safety. If an operation advertises all-or-nothing execution, the underlying implementation must enforce that atomicity across its mutation scope and failure modes. When operations span multiple files or distributed endpoints, partial side effects can occur, and the runtime must report those partial outcomes explicitly in the tool observation. Bundling multi-step work into a single tool call reallocates responsibility from model planning to runtime execution, but the underlying systems obligations remain intact; for the same edit, the shallow composition spends four model calls where the task-level operation spends one (@fig-vol3-deep-vs-shallow-interface).
```

title: Where Each Boundary Acts
caption: **Where Each Boundary Acts**: Two requests steered by the same README text cross mediation, the execution envelope, and egress. The injected `run_shell` request is admitted because it is well typed, then stopped where it tries to read the credential. The dashed segment marks that the destination policy would also refuse its upload, a check on a different part of the path rather than an independent backup. The second request passes every check because each of its steps is permitted, so its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped.
alt: Five columns labeled model proposal, mediation with tool admission, execution envelope with filesystem policy, egress with destination policy, and outside the runtime. Each boundary is drawn as a vertical wall with an opening where a request passes. An injected run_shell request passes the mediation wall, marked admitted, and stops at a solid red block in the execution envelope wall marked read denied; a dashed segment continues to a dashed red block in the egress wall marked upload denied, and a dashed diagnostics box is marked not reached. A submit_report request on the permitted channel passes all three walls, marked admitted, read allowed, and sent, and a red arrow reaches an approved service box marked disclosure.
context:
:::

In the repository scenario, the README text steers two requests through the same boundaries (@fig-vol3-threat-model). The first is the injected `run_shell` command. The second uses a channel the task legitimately holds, because the same README asks the agent to attach source files to the diagnostic report it is permitted to send through a `submit_report` tool. The `run_shell` request is well typed, so tool admission passes it; the filesystem policy then stops it at the read of `~/.aws/credentials`. The destination policy would also refuse its upload, but the two checks guard different things. The read check protects the credential file, and the egress check protects the route out of the host. Neither duplicates the other, so had the credential been readable by some other route, the egress check alone would decide the outcome. The `submit_report` request, carrying private source, passes every gate because each of its steps is allowed, and its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped. Layering boundaries therefore narrows what an attack can do without bounding what a permitted channel can carry, a gap @sec-vol3-sandboxes-permitted-disclosure returns to. Each boundary must also log its decisions, since the absence of an error report is never evidence of safety.

title: Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind
caption: **Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind**: Panel A derives two children from the edit grant. The test grant is rejected because it requests execute, which the parent never held, even though its expiry is earlier. The scan grant is valid because every component is narrower. Deriving it does not remove the edit grant, so a worker that retains the parent can still write until the runtime withdraws it. Panel B shows the chained-caveat alternative, in which each holder narrows a token offline by folding a caveat into the next code, and only a verifier holding the issuer's key can check the whole chain.

Each row shows read, write, and execute slots, filled where the right is held. The parent Gamma_edit, marked still usable, holds read and write over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 300 s. A dashed red branch derives Gamma_test, marked rejected, which holds read and a red execute slot over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 120 s. A solid branch derives Gamma_scan, marked valid, which holds read only over repo/src/pool.py with expiry T0 plus 120 s. Expiry bars start from a shared T0 line, the parent bar longer than the child bars. Panel B, appending a caveat, shows an issuer holding key k, two holders, and a verifier. The token grows from id and sigma 0, to id, c1, and sigma 1, to id, c1, c2, and sigma 2, beside the formulas sigma 0 equals HMAC of k and id, sigma 1 equals HMAC of sigma 0 and c1, and sigma 2 equals HMAC of sigma 1 and c2, with c1 a prefix repo/src/ and c2 rights read. The verifier recomputes k to sigma 0 to sigma 1 to sigma 2 and checks every caveat.
context:
The verifier recomputes the chain of @eq-vol3-macaroon-chain from its root key and admits a request only if every caveat is satisfied. A holder of the child cannot remove a caveat without the prior code $\TokenAuthenticationCode_{i-1}$, which the chain does not reveal, so a subagent or tool worker can narrow authority offline but cannot widen the token it received.

This relation constrains derived authority; a trajectory can still move from inspection to an authorized edit or test phase under explicit policy. Deriving a read-only child also leaves a broader parent that the same holder retained fully usable. If a phase transition is meant to remove write authority, the runtime withdraws or disables the earlier grant and deals with access already opened under it. Delegation must also preserve aggregate budgets: several children together receive at most the parent's resource allowance. Both forms of attenuation share this limit (@fig-vol3-capability-attenuation). A checked derivation narrows what a child may do but leaves the parent usable, and a chained-caveat token narrows what its next holder may do but cannot reach back to restrict a copy of the token someone already holds.

title: Where a System Call Lands
caption: **Where a System Call Lands**: Amber boxes run untrusted code, purple boxes are trusted mediators, and the host kernel closes every column. A shared-kernel container sends every call to the host kernel through a filter. A user-space kernel traps and emulates each call and makes a reduced set of host calls. A microVM's guest kernel handles ordinary calls natively, and only device I/O exits to the monitor. Restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction and reaches the host only through imported functions. The columns differ in which interface untrusted code can reach, not in a ranked probability of escape.
alt: Four columns labeled shared-kernel container, user-space kernel, microVM, and restricted bytecode stand on one host kernel bar that spans all of them. A dashed horizontal line marked trust boundary crosses every column, with amber untrusted boxes above it and purple trusted boxes below it. In the container column, an arrow labeled every call, filtered runs from the workload process through a small filter to the host kernel. In the user-space kernel column, the workload process sends every call, trapped, to a user-space kernel that emulates the call and makes reduced host calls. In the microVM column, guest processes make a native system call to a guest kernel inside a dashed guest region, and a VM exit for device I/O crosses the boundary to the monitor with virtual devices, which makes host calls. In the restricted bytecode column, a module with linear memory reaches a runtime with host imports through imported functions only, and the runtime makes host calls for imports.
context:
:::

Choosing a different envelope changes both the composition of the trusted computing base defined in the threat model and the interface untrusted code can reach. Narrowing that interface simplifies security review, but counting system calls or source lines cannot produce a quantitative probability of sandbox escape. A systems comparison instead asks which failure modes each envelope contains, which components remain trusted, and which operating interfaces the workload requires. The four envelopes in @fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum differ first in where a system call lands: in the host kernel after a filter, in an emulating user-space kernel, in a separate guest kernel, or nowhere at all, because restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction.

title: Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest
caption: **Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest**: The packet filter sees only addresses and ports, so it admits connections to the mediator and drops a direct socket or a lookup sent toward an outside resolver, whatever name the program had in mind. The mediator interprets the request. It resolves its own fixed destinations, admits the repository fetch, and adds the brokered credential, while a push or a request for another repository fails the operation grant at the same hostname. A mediator can inspect or change methods, paths, and bodies only if it makes the upstream request itself or terminates TLS; a proxy that merely forwards encrypted traffic cannot.
alt: Four columns labeled guest with no default route, packet filter that sees addresses and ports, mediator that binds name, operation, and fields, and outside the guest. The packet filter and the mediator are drawn as vertical walls with openings where traffic passes. Four requests leave the guest. A fetch of the approved repo passes the filter to the mediator, is marked fetch admitted with a credential added, and an arrow reaches the approved repository. A push or request for another repo passes the filter to the mediator and stops at a red block in the mediator wall marked operation denied. A direct socket stops at a red block in the filter wall marked dropped, and a dashed metadata host box is marked not reached. A name lookup stops at a red block in the filter wall marked no resolver route, and a dashed external DNS server box is marked not reached.
context:
For any networked guest, routing and protocol enforcement must reside strictly outside the guest's control boundary. Relying on guest-side environment variables such as `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY` fails because an untrusted process can ignore them, bind raw sockets, or establish unauthorized tunnels. Genuine isolation requires the host virtualization layer (using tools such as Linux network namespaces, virtual ethernet pairs, and `nftables` or eBPF cgroup filters) to govern all outbound traffic before it reaches external fabrics.

A comprehensive network boundary reviews every communication vector: direct IP sockets, alternate address families such as IPv6, recursive name-resolution queries, and host services exposed across local virtual bridges. In practice, egress enforcement requires two complementary layers operating in tandem. At the transport and network layer, a packet filter evaluates IP addresses and port numbers. It permits traffic destined exclusively for a designated mediation gateway and drops any direct connection attempt to raw IP literals or external resolvers. At the application layer, a dedicated mediator inspects requested protocols, service paths, and specific operations. Verifying this arrangement demands adversarial testing that confirms attempted bypasses, such as direct socket connections and unbrokered DNS queries, are dropped, rather than only confirming that well-behaved HTTP clients succeed. The two layers fail differently (@fig-vol3-network-egress): the packet filter cannot tell a fetch from a push to the same address, and the mediator never sees a direct socket that the filter has already dropped, so each covers the other's blind spot.

title: A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse
caption: **A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse**: Instances are restored from a trusted baseline into standby, leased to one trajectory, and marked tainted when the lease ends. Reclaiming then follows the reset contract in order: fence the lease's authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore the covered state, and verify that contract. Passing checks return the instance to standby, and a failed check or an incomplete teardown removes it from service. The checks test a defined contract; a clean scan for known residue does not by itself show that every mutable object was covered.

Tainted leads into a reclaiming container with five ordered steps: fence authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore state, and verify reset contract. A red line from every step joins a red path labeled fails that leads to destroyed, marked removed from service. A green arrow labeled contract checks pass runs from the verify step back to standby.

title: Three Connections on One Disclosure Path
caption: **Three Connections on One Disclosure Path**: The fixture disclosure needs private data in reach, attacker-controlled content, and an outbound recipient. Each dashed box weakens or removes one connection at some cost to useful work; when the task needs all three, the dependency and recipient check before dispatch decides whether the query may leave. The three connections describe this injection-driven path, not every possible leak or harm.
alt: A single horizontal path runs from a green private fixture box to a red disclosure-at-service box. Between them, wired in series under a bracket labeled all three on one path, are three thick colored links: private data in reach in green, attacker content in red, and outbound recipient in amber, each crossed by a cut mark; the attacker-content link carries a single tick rather than a double cut, because its control only narrows that link. A dashed lead from each cut mark drops to a dashed box naming the control that can weaken or sever that link: protected test runner, result not bytes; quarantined reader, narrows exposure; and egress boundary, no search. After the third link the path passes through a purple dependency plus recipient check labeled before dispatch, and only a dashed red arrow continues to the disclosure.
context:
:::

EchoLeak and the package-search vulnerability share one topology, the **lethal trifecta**\index{Lethal trifecta!definition} that the sandbox threat model named [@willison2025lethal]: private data in reach, attacker-controlled content in context, and an outbound channel. Severing any one leg closes the exfiltration path. The GitHub MCP leak of @sec-vol3-tool-calling-discovery-authority had the same shape with a public mutation tool in place of the outbound channel and ambient authority as the enabling condition. Containment severs legs by withholding reach. Executing tests inside an isolated runner lets the agent evaluate code against confidential fixtures without loading fixture bytes into the model's context, and an egress boundary can strip network access from subtasks that need no external documentation. Containment cannot handle a workflow that genuinely needs all three legs at once. There, a dependency-and-recipient check before dispatch must arbitrate each outbound request, distinguishing legitimate local processing from release (@fig-vol3-exfiltration-conjunction).

where $\AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)$ is the set of sources the task policy accepts as influences on $\ProposedOperation$. The first condition is the release check and the second is the evidence check; they fail independently. A local test run can accept candidate code from any source, so its $\AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)$ is unrestricted, while recording a test pass for acceptance admits only the protected runner. caption: **The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness**: Panel (a) runs the model's proposed call directly and keeps all state in the message list, so an outside request has nowhere to land, nothing bounds cumulative spend, and calls that policy would gate run at once.
