section: The anatomy of an unmanaged loop {#sec-vol3-harness-unmanaged-loop}
context:
:::

Because an unmanaged loop lacks an independent, externally accessible control state, it cannot support the operational requirements of production systems. If an operator must pause an execution run while a long test suite executes, the runtime provides no interface to receive that command. If cumulative token consumption exhausts the allocated budget, the loop cannot withhold the next model call without terminating abruptly and abandoning in-flight work. Any tool invocation proposed by the model also executes immediately under ambient authority, bypassing policy checks or human review. Although a supervised harness may also execute as a loop or coroutine, it wraps that loop in an explicit state machine with invariant rules governing every continuation path, so that every proposal is filtered before any tool call is admitted (@fig-vol3-controlplane-arch).

title: Trajectory State Machine
caption: **Trajectory State Machine**: Five live states, a finalizing state, and three terminal outcomes. The ordinary cycle runs from READY through CALLING_MODEL and WAITING_TOOL back to READY; a proposal that policy requires reviewed is held in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and pause is entered only from READY. Every exit passes through FINALIZING, which stops admission and resolves or transfers remaining duties before an absorbing terminal state. Each arrow is a guarded edge, and events such as a late result or a usage report can update the record's operation table without changing state.
alt: State diagram. A dashed live-states region holds PAUSED above READY, CALLING_MODEL to the right of READY, WAITING_TOOL below READY, and AWAITING_APPROVAL, drawn dashed, below CALLING_MODEL. Heavy arrows trace the ordinary cycle: call admitted from READY to CALLING_MODEL, tool call admitted to WAITING_TOOL, and wait policy met back to READY. Lighter arrows show pause and resume between READY and PAUSED, no admissible action from CALLING_MODEL to READY, approval required from CALLING_MODEL to AWAITING_APPROVAL, approved and guards pass to WAITING_TOOL, and a dashed path for denied, expired, or stale requests returning a refused observation to READY. A completion request arrow and a dashed arrow from any live state for cancel, kill, budget, or deadline lead to FINALIZING, which branches to three double-bordered absorbing states: COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELED.
context:
: **Reply Status and Next State**: Every non-completed status returns to a state that admits no dispatch from the failed reply; reservations for failed or faulted calls stay outstanding until usage settles. {#tbl-vol3-harness-status-routing tbl-colwidths="[34,20,46]"}

Action approval introduces a controlled detour to this cycle. An approved action transitions from `AWAITING_APPROVAL` to `WAITING_TOOL` only when its active dispatch guards pass; recording operator approval does not automatically execute the tool. Conversely, a denial, expiration, or operator withdrawal emits a refusal observation back to `READY`.

title: The Approval Gate
caption: **The Approval Gate**: Panel (a) lists what the reviewer approves for the r18 review submission: the exact proposal, its destination and data scope, the selected evidence with its limited scope, the preconditions, the digest that binds the approval, the expiry, and the requesting trajectory. Panel (b) holds the proposal without sending it, obtains a decision the model takes no part in, and rechecks current conditions at the dispatch boundary. An approval without capacity stays held; a denial, expiry, or stale proposal returns a refusal observation.
alt: Two stacked panels. Panel (a) is a record: a top cell holding the exact proposal, submit_review with the r18 patch and named check records, above a row of five cells for destination, evidence, preconditions, expiry, and requesting trajectory, each tied by a short line to a bar below labeled approval digest, which binds the proposal and every field. Panel (b) shows steps 1 hold, labeled AWAITING_APPROVAL, 2 reviewer, and 3 decision in a row, followed by a vertical bar labeled 4 recheck at the dispatch boundary with a single opening. Only the approved and current path passes through the opening to WAITING_TOOL. An approved request with no capacity loops back to hold, a denied or expired decision drops to a REFUSED box that returns to READY, and a stale request at the boundary also goes to REFUSED.
context:
After validating a completed model response, the harness records the held proposal before publishing its approval request. The record references the task and requester, intended tool origin and operation, immutable candidate artifact and selected evidence, applicable preconditions, required approver policy, and approval expiry. It also assigns an approval-request identifier and a held-proposal version, and computes the **approval digest**\index{Approval digest!definition}, the digest that action-bound approval binds, computed here over the canonical held proposal and covering the operation, its arguments, its target, and the versions of the referenced artifacts. The approval binds to that digest, so changing any argument or artifact produces a different digest and voids the approval. These identifiers and the cryptographic digest track the pending decision itself, distinct from the logical operation IDs or transport-layer idempotency tokens assigned once dispatch begins.

For the review submission, the held artifact is the exact `r18` patch and named check records, not a mutable filesystem path whose contents can shift before execution. The selected records retain their evidential scope; a targeted unit-test pass does not become full acceptance because it appears in an approval request. The authentication and represented-action requirements are those of action-bound approval. The harness adds the recorded status needed to distinguish pending, denied, expired, withdrawn, and admitted requests. @Fig-vol3-human-escrow diagrams this approval pipeline: panel (a) binds the exact proposal payload, artifact hashes, destination scope, and expiration timestamp into an immutable approval digest for revision `r18`, while panel (b) traces the four-step resolution sequence that parks the trajectory in `AWAITING_APPROVAL` until reviewer decisions and dispatch guards are verified.

title: The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log
caption: **The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log**: The record in runtime memory (top) is lost on a crash; the durable, append-only log (bottom) is not. Folding the logged events through a deterministic reducer, starting from the initial record $\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0$, rebuilds the recorded projection $\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_j$ at boundary $\LogPositionIndex$ without calling the model or any tool. Because the log ends at the test's recorded intent with no recorded result, the reconstructed record keeps the admission and reservation and marks the test unresolved rather than inventing its outcome.
alt: Two regions. Top region, runtime memory lost on a crash, drawn with a dashed border: an initial record R zero with rows for task, grants, limits and no admitted operations; a deterministic reducer applying apply of R and e with no model or tool call; and a reconstructed record R j with rows admission held, reservation held, and a dashed red row test r18 unresolved. Bottom region, the durable append-only trajectory log, drawn as a contiguous tape of cells labeled e1 TaskStarted, e2 ContextBuilt, e3 ModelReplied, e4 Authorized and BudgetReserved, and e j ToolIntent test r18, then a vertical line labeled boundary j and a dashed cell for a ToolResult that was not recorded. An arrow labeled fold, in log order runs up from the log to the reducer, and a red dotted line links the unrecorded ToolResult to the unresolved row.
context:
In this formulation, $\LogPositionIndex$ indexes the durable log sequence boundary rather than the interaction turn $\TurnIndex$. Given deterministic reducer semantics and complete event payloads, folding reconstructs the precise control state without invoking the foundation model or re-executing external tools. This architecture embodies the classic **event sourcing**\index{Event sourcing!definition} pattern [@kleppmann2017designing]: historical decisions serve as deterministic inputs to state reconstruction, while unrecorded events remain explicitly unknown. If the latest durable log entry indicates that a test execution was authorized and dispatched, but contains no corresponding completion event, the reconstructed state marks that operation as unresolved (@fig-vol3-event-sourcing). For the worksheet crash, the fold keeps the held reservation and the dispatched `test_r18` intent, and it invents no outcome for the test.

[^fn-append-log-lineage]: **Append-Only Log as Primary Record**: Rosenblum and Ousterhout's log-structured file system treated the sequential log as the primary on-disk data structure, accelerating write throughput and simplifying crash recovery [@rosenblum1992lfs]. A trajectory log inherits these exact advantages: append operations never overwrite historical evidence required by future recovery passes, allowing a recovering worker to reconstruct state by streaming an ordered log rather than reconciling conflicting in-place updates. \index{Log-structured file system!append-only trajectory log}

title: Intent Before Dispatch
caption: **Intent Before Dispatch**: The runtime validates a proposal, admits it with a reservation, and waits for the intent's acknowledgment under the declared failure domain before dispatch carries the request past the durability barrier. Where a crash falls determines the recovery state of @tbl-vol3-durable-recovery-states. Before the worker receives the acknowledgment, dispatch is withheld, but the intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. An absent intent establishes non-dispatch only when the authoritative prefix is complete. Between the acknowledgment and adequate recorded evidence, including a crash before dispatch, the operation is in doubt; a pending or timeout observation leaves it there. After correlated outcome evidence is recorded, the outcome is established within the endpoint's contract.
alt: A row of five ordered event boxes: e prop, proposal; e auth, admission; e flush, intent ack; a ext, dispatch, in amber; and e obs, evidence. A dashed vertical line labeled durability barrier separates e flush from a ext, with runtime can still withhold on its left and request may have left on its right. Below, a time axis is marked at e flush and e obs, and three bands show the recovery state if the crash falls there: a gray band before e flush, not dispatched, intent may be durable; a red band from e flush to e obs, in doubt, withhold dependent work, which the barrier line crosses; and a green band after e obs, established, per endpoint contract.

In @eq-vol3-wal-ordering, $\ValidatedProposalEvent$ is the validated complete proposal, $\AdmissionDecisionEvent$ is the admitted authorization and reservation decision, and $\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent$ acknowledges its recoverable `ToolIntent` and required preceding records under the declared failure domain. The action $\ExternalDispatchAction$ is dispatch, not endpoint completion. The event $\EvidenceRecordEvent$ is the later durable recording of received evidence, whose status may still be pending, partial, or unknown. The ordering constrains the events that occur; an attempt can stop before dispatch or never produce evidence. Its payoff is that the position of a crash in this sequence determines what recovery may conclude (@fig-vol3-intent-before-dispatch). A crash before the worker receives $\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent$ means the attempt was never dispatched, but an intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. Recovery must inspect the complete authoritative prefix to determine whether that intent survived. A crash after $\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent$ but before adequate outcome evidence becomes durable leaves an **in-doubt action**\index{In-doubt action!definition}, an admitted operation whose outcome the surviving evidence cannot settle. This includes a crash before dispatch or after a pending or timeout observation. It is the tool layer's uncertain outcome (definition \ref{dfn-uncertain-outcome}) seen from the recovery side, and it is what the fold of @sec-vol3-durable-execution-log-evidence marked unresolved. Only recorded, correlated evidence establishes an outcome.

title: Live Execution vs. Replay

$$\RepairSuccessProbability > \RepairSuccessProbability^* = \frac{\RepairAttemptCost}{\FallbackCost}.$$ {#eq-vol3-repair-breakeven}

Engineers must evaluate this comparison independently for latency (in seconds) and monetary expense (in model dollars), as their respective break-even thresholds $\RepairSuccessProbability^*$ often diverge. If $\RepairAttemptCost \ge \FallbackCost$, no success probability below one can make repair cheaper on that resource axis. Furthermore, if a failed repair alters residual side effects, extends resource holding times, or increases fallback complexity, the term $(1-\RepairSuccessProbability)\FallbackCost$ must be replaced by the corresponding conditional fallback cost. ensuring that an uncooperative or persistently degraded dependency receives geometrically fewer probe attempts up to the ceiling $\MaximumBreakerCooldownInterval$. If a delayed response from an earlier probe generation eventually succeeds, that late arrival can settle its own operation record and its charges, but the generation guard prevents it from closing the newly reopened breaker or usurping a newer trial's slot.

title: Verdict-Aware Trace Selection
caption: **Verdict-Aware Trace Selection**: Trace bodies pass a fallible minimization boundary into a bounded buffer that holds them until task verdicts, which can arrive late, reach the selector. Selection applies a declared precedence among the classes of @tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies, keeps inclusion probabilities with retained traces, and discards unselected bodies. Every admitted trial also enters the accounting record directly, together with recorded drops, evictions, and truncation, so the denominator does not depend on which bodies survived. Assigning high retention priority protects failure traces under moderate load, though severe buffer saturation can still force evictions before verdicts arrive.
alt: Left-to-right flow diagram. An admitted-trials box sends traces through a dashed amber capture boundary, labeled minimize, redact, into a green bounded buffer drawn as a row of eight slots, some shaded red for failures, some dashed for pending verdicts, one gray, the rest plain, held until verdict. One plain slot drops below the buffer, labeled evicted. The buffer feeds a selection precedence ladder that also receives late task verdicts from above. Its four numbered rungs are failed or violation, shaded red; pending or unknown, dashed; accepted, slow or costly, gray; and ordinary accepted, plain, matching the slot styles. The ladder sends selected traces to a violet trace store that keeps inclusion probability and, from its bottom edge, unselected traces to a dashed discarded box. Along the bottom, a violet evaluation accounting record spans the width, receiving an arrow labeled every trial straight from admitted trials and a red dashed arrow from the evicted slot labeled drops, evictions, truncation.
context:
:::

Physical buffer limits inevitably govern this architecture. Buffer managers must enforce four concurrent bounds: active trace count, aggregate byte volume, individual trace size limits, and maximum staging age. Sizing from averages, such as mean concurrent traces multiplied by mean trace size, is a frequent engineering trap, because cascading failures typically produce bursts of unusually long, tool-heavy trajectories that quickly exhaust buffer memory. Telemetry systems must expose real-time metrics for head-dropped records, buffer evictions, and span truncations broken down by cohort and selection class. Without this visibility, correlated loss during incidents will silently purge the exact failure traces engineers need to diagnose system outages. Furthermore, while deferred tail selection curtails long-term downstream storage, it does not reduce the network ingress and memory needed to buffer traces prior to selection, and strict privacy restrictions apply to these staging buffers as well. The accounting record therefore sits outside the buffer (@fig-vol3-tail-sampling-pipeline). Every admitted trial enters it directly, together with every recorded drop, eviction, and truncation, so the denominator survives whatever the buffer loses.

Staging separates evidence available before live execution from evidence that requires it. title: Probes Before Weights
caption: **Probes Before Weights**: Under the default diagnostic route, counterfactual probes evaluate a measured failure in ascending ladder order. A failure that disappears under a probe routes to an immediate systems repair, modifying versioned artifacts that revert cleanly as configuration. Only failures that survive every lower-rung probe reach the weight modification stages, where supervised fine-tuning precedes reinforcement learning. Engineering cost rises and operational reversibility falls from top to bottom.

Red arrows labeled persists link the probes. From each probe an arrow labeled disappears leads right to a repair box under the heading repair below the weights: repair context, retrieval or assembly; repair tool or schema, schema, docs, or adapter; and repair runtime, bounds, sandbox pool, recovery. A red arrow labeled survives every probe crosses a dashed horizontal boundary to a red residual failure box, plausibly behavioral, which leads on evidence to supervised fine-tuning, curated residual corpus, and then down to reinforcement learning, rollouts, protected reward check, under the heading change the weights. context:
be implemented completely and correctly. A typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}) provides enforceable guarantees across any model version placed behind it. By contrast, fine-tuning a model to guess fields omitted by an API schema instills brittle behavioral habits that collapse as soon as the interface evolves. For example, an integration test on an observation adapter can verify that truncated outputs return explicit pagination markers, resolving ambiguity at the interface layer without requiring downstream models to compensate for incomplete schemas.

Rigorous empirical evidence, rather than administrative convention, governs when a failure ascends the ladder. Engineers evaluate each lower rung using a **counterfactual probe**\index{Counterfactual probe!definition}: a controlled re-execution of the recorded failure trace with that rung's suspected defect artificially removed. For a context defect, the probe injects the missing fact directly into the prompt. For an interface ambiguity, it resumes matched saved prefixes with corrected tool descriptions or schemas and samples fresh continuations under the controlled conditions of @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor. Replaying a fixed proposal instead tests the validation or adapter boundary; it does not measure whether the model chooses a different action. For a runtime failure, it executes the identical tool payload within an isolated sandbox with relaxed resource limits. If the failure disappears under a given probe, the result supports a repair at that system rung under the probed conditions without ruling out other contributing causes. Under this default diagnostic route, only the residual failures that persist across all lower-level counterfactual probes advance to the learning pipeline. Probing in ladder order routes each resolved defect to an immediate, reversible repair, so only the failures that survive all three probes reach the weights (@fig-vol3-failure-diagnostic-tree). Even then, candidate checkpoints trained on this residual must be validated under the protocol of @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor rather than accepted merely because model weights were the final hypothesis remaining.

A preference route adds the shared-context and justified-ordering conditions that define a preference comparison (@sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-learning-artifacts) to its outcome and target predicates. Until paired with an appropriate winning rollout, a failed attempt remains merely an unassigned comparison candidate. For reinforcement learning pipelines, curation delivers versioned task definitions, deterministic environment fixtures, and automated grading harnesses for fresh rollouts rather than static records of historical failures. While these downstream applications share uniform requirements for permitted use ($\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$) and record adequacy ($\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$), they diverge sharply in how they evaluate outcomes ($\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$) and assign target labels ($\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$).

Each predicate evaluates to one of four canonical states: `pass`, `fail`, `pending`, or `unknown`, aligning with the four-verdict rule formalized in @sec-vol3-evaluation-contract-verdicts. An explicit `fail` immediately halts evaluation along that route and keeps the record for diagnosis or another route (@fig-vol3-verifier-cascade). A missing or timed-out check never defaults to a pass; unverified candidates move to an unresolved quarantine holding queue, tagged with the missing evidence and execution logs required for resolution. Curation telemetry tracks the counts of evaluated, admitted, rejected, and unresolved records per route, ensuring that trajectories redirected to diagnostic pools never inflate the reported yield of production demonstrations.

title: Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples
caption: **Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples**: Two independent examples share one buffer. Under an ordinary causal mask (a), every query in the second example scores keys in the first, so the second example can use context it will not have when served. The block-diagonal mask (b) keeps causal scores only inside each example and sets every cross-example entry to $-\infty$ before the softmax, as in @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention. The boundary offsets define the blocks; whether a kernel also skips the masked blocks is an implementation property.

In panel a, the lower triangle within each example is shaded as a score, the remaining upper cells are gray minus infinity, and the block where example 2 queries meet example 1 keys is shaded red and labeled leak. In panel b, the same lower triangles are shaded, the whole cross-example block is gray and labeled minus infinity, and the key axis carries the boundary offsets 0, s 1, and s 1 plus s 2. A legend defines the score, minus infinity before softmax, and cross-example score.
context:
Under an ordinary causal mask, every query in a later example can score keys in an earlier one; the block-diagonal mask sets each of those cross-example entries to $-\infty$ before the softmax, and excludes trailing padding keys the same way (@fig-vol3-block-diagonal-mask). Variable-length attention kernels [@dao2023flashattention2] enforce this without materializing a dense $-\infty$ matrix. The loader hands the kernel the example boundaries as cumulative offsets, $0$, $\PackedExampleLength_1$, $\PackedExampleLength_1+\PackedExampleLength_2$, and so on through the buffer's total length ($\BatchSize+1$ entries for $\BatchSize$ examples), so that example $\PackedExampleIndex$ occupies one contiguous interval of positions, and the kernel computes scores only for query and key pairs that fall inside the same interval. Whether a given kernel also skips the computation for cross-example blocks of the score matrix, and how much time that saves, is an implementation property to measure on the target accelerator. The mask is the correctness requirement; skipped work is a throughput bonus that must be shown, not assumed.

The equivalence is the property to test: a packed loader that trains faster but lets examples read one another has changed the learning problem, and no loss curve will show it.

title: Four Coordination Arrangements
caption: **Four Coordination Arrangements**: Each panel shows where work crosses a boundary. A supervisor sends envelopes down and collects receipts, a pipeline passes artifacts through bounded queues, a blackboard mediates claims and versioned publications through a shared store, and actors exchange addressed messages through mailboxes. One supervisor round costs $2\WorkerCount$ deliveries and a full mesh round $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$. Each topology imposes specific runtime obligations for bounding queues, isolating concurrent state, and verifying result correctness.
alt: Four panels. Panel a: a wide supervisor box above three worker boxes, each worker with a downward solid envelope arrow and an upward dashed receipt arrow, labeled 2N per round. Panel b: stage 1, stage 2, and stage 3 in a row, separated by two bounded queues drawn as three slots each, partly occupied, with artifacts passing through them. Panel c: three worker boxes sending claim and publish arrows to a shared store holding task 2 claimed and artifact versions 2 and 3, with dashed read arrows back. Panel d: four actor boxes, each with a small mailbox of slots, joined by faint dashed links of the possible full mesh, labeled N times N minus 1, with three solid addressed messages drawn on it.
context:
Message counts scale with the communication graph and its interaction protocol. If each of $\WorkerCount$ participants transmits an update to every other participant during an execution round, the network must handle $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$ directed deliveries. With an average payload size of $\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength$ tokens per delivery, that single round consumes $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength$ tokens across the system. In contrast, a supervisor managing $\WorkerCount$ workers requires only $2\WorkerCount$ deliveries per round (one dispatch envelope and one receipt per worker), consuming $2\WorkerCount{}\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength$ tokens. The full mesh thus scales quadratically, transmitting $(\WorkerCount-1)/2$ times more messages per round than the centralized coordinator.

Raw transmission volume measures network traffic, not what the receiving models must ingest. In a fully connected mesh where each agent appends every incoming peer message to its prompt history, ingested tokens per round grow as $\mathcal{O}(\WorkerCount^2)$, and the append-only re-send of @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend compounds that growth across rounds because each later prompt carries every earlier delivery. Even in a centralized topology, verbose receipts, iterative deliberation rounds, or frequent status polling against a blackboard store can exhaust context windows and inflate inference budgets. Across the four arrangements of @fig-vol3-multi-agent-topologies, the supervisor's round costs $2\WorkerCount$ deliveries and the actor mesh up to $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$, while the pipeline and blackboard replace direct deliveries with bounded queues and versioned claims that the runtime must police.

title: Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree
caption: **Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree**: Under the one-for-one policy (a), only the failed worker restarts, as a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, while its siblings continue. Under the one-for-all policy (b), the supervisor stops the coupled siblings through the cancellation protocol and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs, because the caller's partial work has lost its meaning. Either supervisor that exceeds its declared restart intensity stops restarting and escalates the failure to its parent.

Card b, one_for_all: a supervisor with interface, caller, and test children all inside one dashed red blast radius; caller is marked failed, interface and test are marked stopped, and arrows from all three lead to one box labeled group restarts, new attempts from recorded inputs. A dashed red arrow from supervisor b to the parent is labeled restart intensity exceeded, escalate.
context:
[^fn-erlang-supervisor-trees]: **Erlang Supervision Trees**\index{Supervision tree!Erlang/OTP}: Erlang emerged from a telephone-switching research program initiated in 1981, established on the design principle that systems should allow failing processes to crash cleanly while a designated supervisor restores known-good state, rather than attempting defensive error handling locally [@armstrong2003making]. In agentic systems, this principle is even more vital: allowing a confused agent trajectory to attempt local recovery within a contaminated context window frequently compounds its errors, whereas a supervisor restart provisions a clean execution context from recorded inputs.

To prevent degenerate retry storms, supervision trees enforce a **restart intensity**\index{Restart intensity!definition} bound, the maximum number of restarts permitted within a sliding time window. When a child agent repeatedly fails and breaches this threshold, the supervisor ceases local restarts, aborts its remaining subordinates, and escalates the failure upward to its own parent supervisor. In an agentic system, a restart must never simply continue from the failed worker's corrupted or circular context window. Instead, the runtime treats each restart as a freshly admitted attempt, provisioning a clean context initialized from recorded input artifacts and acquiring a fresh budget reservation. When aborting sibling processes under `one_for_all` or escalation, the runtime invokes the structured cancellation and cleanup protocols described in @sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure.

context:
The mixture model also bounds what ensemble scaling can achieve. Conditional on a candidate's propensity $\FalseApprovalPropensity$, the weak law of large numbers implies that the fraction of reviewers falsely approving converges to $\FalseApprovalPropensity$ as the ensemble grows. Consequently, an arbitrarily large majority vote falsely approves precisely those candidates with $\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2$. Rather than decaying toward zero, majority false approval approaches a nonzero asymptotic floor at $\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)$.

Under the parameters modeled in the notebook, that floor is `{python} ReviewFloor.floor_str`. At `{python} ReviewFloor.large_ensemble_str` reviewers, independent errors would reduce majority false approvals to `{python} ReviewFloor.independent_large_str`, whereas the beta mixture leaves the error rate stalled at `{python} ReviewFloor.mixture_large_str`. In @fig-vol3-correlated-ensemble-failure the independent curve keeps falling toward zero while the mixture curve flattens just above the floor, and at five reviewers the mixture moves probability to the extremes, so a candidate is approved by no one or by a majority far more often than independence predicts. Tripling the committee from five to `{python} ReviewFloor.large_ensemble_str` reviewers of the same kind triples review spend yet lowers majority false approval only from `{python} ReviewCorrelation.mixture_majority_str` to `{python} ReviewFloor.mixture_large_str`, because the remaining errors concentrate on candidates that every such model finds difficult.
